evaluated.name: Weakest-Link Cheap And Profitable
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Mispricing requires both cheapness and operating quality; a firm should be rewarded only by whichever attribute is weaker, so that extreme cheapness cannot compensate for weak cash profitability and vice versa.
evaluated.reasoning: Taking the minimum of the two ranks implements a strict conjunctive screen that is not spanned by any additive value or quality composite, since it penalizes attribute imbalance rather than averaging it away. The long leg is populated by firms cheap on cash-earnings yield AND persistently cash-profitable, while deep-value distress names and expensive high-quality compounders are both excluded.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry Sales Yield With Margin Improvement
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A low price-to-sales relative to industry peers predicts returns only when gross profitability is trending up; when margins are deteriorating the depressed sales multiple correctly prices a decaying franchise.
evaluated.reasoning: Sales-to-price is the valuation multiple least contaminated by accounting choices, and the five-year gross-profitability trend supplies a directional quality state that separates recovering cheap firms from structurally impaired ones. Both legs are industry-ranked so the interaction is measured within peer groups, avoiding a mechanical sector bet toward low-margin industries.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Solvency-Gated Enterprise Earnings Yield
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(re, at), 0), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at)), -0.3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A high operating earnings yield is evidence of mispricing only for firms that can survive to realize it; if retained earnings are negative or net debt is large relative to assets, the low price is compensation for solvency risk rather than a mispricing, so the valuation signal should be switched off entirely.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the earlier additive rank average with an explicit multiplicative gate: the quality/solvency variables no longer contribute their own return premium at all, they only decide whether the valuation signal is transmitted, which is exactly the conditional language of the hypothesis. It is the mirror image of Signal 1 (there valuation gates quality, here solvency gates valuation), the thresholds are unit-free accounting ratios with non-zero denominators (at), and distressed cheap names are pushed to a neutral zero rather than into the long leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Non-Cash Charge Valuation Wedge
evaluated.expression: SUB(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that look far cheaper on cash earnings than on reported net income have earnings depressed by heavy non-cash depreciation charges; that gap is conservative accounting quality, not economic weakness, and the market underprices the hidden cash generation.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs are valuation ranks, so the spread is close to HML-neutral by construction and its abnormal return cannot come from a simple cheapness bet — the only surviving content is the depreciation wedge, which FF5 does not price. Industry ranking prevents the signal from becoming a pure capital-intensity sector tilt, and the difference form avoids the doubly-bad-corner problem of rank products.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Own-History Cheapness With Intact Margins
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5)), INDICATOR(DELTA(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3), 1), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm trading at the cheap end of its own five-year valuation range is mispriced only if its operating margins have not deteriorated; identical own-history cheapness accompanied by falling gross profitability is a rational repricing of a decaying franchise.
evaluated.reasoning: Time-series cheapness is close to orthogonal to the cross-sectional book-to-market that HML spans, which directly addresses the negative-alpha problem of the archive, and the smoothed gross-margin change supplies the quality state that decides whether the de-rating is information or overreaction. Standardizing the time-series rank keeps the passing group signed while margin-deteriorating firms are set to neutral rather than shorted, avoiding a short leg dominated by transient losers.

evaluated.name: Glamour With Working-Capital Bloat
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The sharpest valuation-quality mispricing sits on the overpriced side: firms carrying a rich price relative to the gross profit they actually generate, while simultaneously inflating net working capital, are financing an expensive valuation with soft, reversing accounting numbers and should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than swapping a gate inside the same yield×indicator template, this flips the economic side of the interaction: the informative corner is expensive-plus-deteriorating-quality, which is where limits to arbitrage bind hardest and where FF5's HML and RMW have the least power because both legs are ranked within industry. Using NEG of the gross-profit yield rather than the inverted multiple keeps negative-gross-profit firms at the expensive extreme instead of flipping their sign, and the product of two non-negative industry ranks makes the top corner unambiguously the doubly-bad firm.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Multiple Agreement Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness is credible only when independent accounting bases agree: a firm cheap on book value but expensive on gross profit is an asset-heavy business with no earning power, while a firm cheap on gross profit but expensive on book has already written its assets up; only agreement across both bases identifies genuine underpricing.
evaluated.reasoning: Price appears in both legs and they are combined with a non-linear MIN rather than a difference, so the scaling does not cancel and the construct cannot collapse to gross-profits-to-assets — the object measured is disagreement across multiples, a dimension RMW does not represent. The quality content enters through which fundamental the market is being asked to capitalize (gross profit versus book assets), so the long leg is cheap-and-earning rather than merely cheap.

evaluated.name: Cheap And Retiring Net Obligations
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(lt, che), at), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A depressed valuation resolves into returns when the firm is actively shrinking its net obligations: deleveraging transfers enterprise value to equity holders, whereas a cheap firm whose net liabilities keep rising is transferring value to creditors and is a genuine trap.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the binary yield×indicator template for a continuous product of two non-negative industry ranks, so no firm is parked at an artificial zero and portfolio composition stays stable across time. The quality channel is the change in cash-netted total obligations rather than a static solvency level or a working-capital accrual, which makes it distinct from both the archived solvency gate and the accrual-based proposals, and only loosely related to CMA's asset-growth content.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Obligation-Netted Fundamental To Price
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(che, lt), MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: What equity holders can actually claim is cash, minus all obligations, plus a durable cash-earnings stream; a market capitalization that is small relative to that claim indicates underpricing, whereas a firm whose apparent cheapness disappears once liabilities are netted and earnings are averaged is priced correctly.
evaluated.reasoning: Dividends are dropped entirely, which removes the non-payer zero mass and the dependence on a published payout anomaly, and coverage becomes near-universal since cash, liabilities and cash earnings are reported by essentially all firms. The quality element is structural rather than a bolt-on screen: obligations are subtracted from the numerator and the earnings component is a three-year average, so a single peak year or a liability-financed balance sheet cannot generate a high score.

evaluated.name: Net Cash Cheapness With Real Gross Profit
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A large net-cash position relative to market value signals undervaluation only when the firm runs a genuinely profitable operating business; in cash-burning shells the same net-cash yield reflects a melting asset and predicts poor returns, which is why unfiltered net-cash cheapness has a perverse cross-sectional slope.
evaluated.reasoning: It keeps the balance-sheet channel that produced the archive's only positive FF5 alpha but repairs its diagnosed defect by requiring three-year average gross profitability, a persistent quality state that shells cannot fake. Both legs are non-negative industry ranks, so the top corner is unambiguously cash-rich-and-profitable and the bottom corner is levered-and-unprofitable, which is exactly the quality-value versus value-trap partition.

evaluated.name: Cheapness Amplified By Cash-Backing Persistence
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(oancf, ib), 0), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: What distinguishes quality value is not the level of earnings quality in one year but its repetition: a cheap firm whose operating cash flow has exceeded reported earnings in most of the last five years has demonstrably conservative accounting, while a single clean year is uninformative.
evaluated.reasoning: The quality leg is a persistence count in {0,...,5} rather than a level or a gate, so it amplifies cheapness continuously without creating a zero mass, and habitual conservatism is a state no FF5 factor represents. Pairing it with gross-profit-to-price rather than book-to-market keeps the valuation leg tied to an income statement line that accrual management cannot easily distort.

evaluated.name: Obligation-Heavy Discount With Fading Margins
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The classic value trap is a firm whose equity is small relative to the obligations stacked ahead of it and whose operating margins are trending down; such firms look cheap on equity multiples precisely because the residual claim is being eroded, and they should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning: This targets the trap leg directly using liabilities-to-price — a valuation of the obligation stack rather than of the equity fundamentals — interacted with a five-year margin trend, giving a short-side mechanism that is the economic complement of Signals 1 and 2's unlevered long side. Testing both corners in the same generation identifies whether the FF5 alpha in this family comes from avoiding traps or from owning cash-rich quality.

evaluated.name: Owner Earnings Yield After Working-Capital Funding
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), MA(DELTA(SUB(act, lct), 1), 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: What an owner can actually take out is cash earnings less the working capital the business must keep funding; a cheap firm whose reported profits are consumed by growing receivables and inventory is a value trap, while a cheap firm whose earnings survive the working-capital charge is genuinely underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning:
Rather than re-ranking an existing archive expression, this changes the numerator's economic content: the quality theme enters by deducting the balance-sheet investment (act, lct) required to sustain earnings, so two firms with identical earnings yields are separated by whether their profits are self-financing. Three-year averaging of both the cash-earnings and the working-capital-investment legs keeps the measure a durable state rather than a one-year accrual reading, and the ratio is monotone with near-universal coverage.

HYPOTHESIS_END

evaluated.name: De-Rating Beyond Fundamental Deterioration
evaluated.expression: SUB(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: Mispricing arises when the market marks a firm down further than its own fundamentals have fallen; a firm whose gross-profit yield is at the high end of its five-year range while its gross profitability is not at the low end of its own range has been de-rated by sentiment rather than by deteriorating quality.
evaluated.reasoning:
This abandons the rejected conjunctive MIN design entirely and instead compares two firm-level time-series positions — valuation history against operating-quality history — so both legs are self-referential and neither is a cross-sectional cheapness or profitability bet that HML and RMW can span. Because the gross-profit numerator is common to both legs, the difference isolates the price-versus-fundamental divergence, which is precisely the overreaction the value-trap story predicts should revert.
REASONING_END

evaluated.name: Earned Capital Per Dollar Of Total Claims
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(re, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Book value that was earned and retained is evidence of a long profit history, whereas book value contributed by investors is not; a firm carrying deep retained earnings relative to the entire stack of claims on it — market equity plus all liabilities — is cheap for quality reasons, while a firm with thin or negative earned capital priced at the same multiple is cheap because it has never generated value.
evaluated.reasoning:
This drops the twice-used yield×quality-rank product for a single monotone ratio in which the quality theme defines the numerator (earned rather than contributed capital) and the valuation theme, together with the obligation stack, defines the denominator, so leverage cannot manufacture apparent cheapness. The denominator is strictly positive, avoiding the sign discontinuities that plagued earlier ratio attempts, coverage is essentially universal, and negative-retained-earnings firms sort to the short leg where the distress story places them.
REASONING_END

evaluated.name: Net Cash Cheapness With Liability Coverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, lt), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What makes cash-rich cheapness durable is that the operating business can also service the obligations it does carry; cash-flow coverage of total liabilities, rather than the level of margin, is the quality state that distinguishes a mispriced balance sheet from one whose cash is already spoken for.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's best signal pairs the net-cash valuation leg with gross-profits-to-assets, a quantity RMW largely spans, so the critic's concern that the profitability leg carries the load is testable by swapping in a solvency-flow quality measure that FF5 does not represent. If the alpha survives or improves, the mispricing is about balance-sheet safety rather than profitability level; if it collapses, the profitability channel was doing the work.

evaluated.name: Cheapness Backed By Liquid Assets
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(act, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A low price-to-book is credible when the book value sits in current assets that can be converted or redeployed, and is suspect when it sits in long-lived operating assets whose carrying value depends on the same weak business the market is discounting; asset composition therefore determines whether book value is a floor or an accounting artifact.
evaluated.reasoning: Asset-composition quality is an untested channel here and is conceptually distinct from profitability, leverage and accruals — it speaks to the reliability of the denominator in the valuation ratio rather than to the income statement. It also offers a cheap, high-coverage test of whether the alpha in the net-cash family generalises to liquidity of the whole asset base rather than cash specifically.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap With Interest-Free Financing Mix
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What makes a discount dangerous is not the size of a firm's obligations but their type: trade payables and accrued expenses are interest-free, renegotiable financing that reflects supplier bargaining power, whereas interest-bearing debt carries fixed dates that can force liquidation before a mispricing corrects, so cheap firms whose liabilities are predominantly non-financial should realise the value premium.
evaluated.reasoning:
This replaces the incoherent che-minus-lt construction with the obligation *composition* rather than its level, so the quality leg is a bounded share in [0,1] with a clear economic reading and no dependence on cash being large relative to liabilities. It tests a distinct hypothesis from the archive's net-cash signal — that the trap mechanism is the hardness of the claim, not the absence of claims — and the two together identify whether cash buffers or claim softness drive the observed alpha.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cheap With Compounding Earned Capital Per Share
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(re, csho), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The quality that redeems a low valuation is per-share accumulation of earned capital: a cheap firm whose retained earnings per share have compounded over three years is quietly building shareholder value, while a cheap firm whose earned capital per share is flat or shrinking is either losing money or diluting existing holders to stay funded.
evaluated.reasoning:
Rather than restating the net-external-financing anomaly as a standalone leg, dilution enters only through the per-share denominator of a value-creation measure, so a firm that issues shares while growing earned capital faster still scores well — the signal reads capital creation net of dilution, not issuance itself. This makes the quality state a cumulative outcome variable (retained profit per share) rather than a financing action, which is the conditioning the value-trap story actually requires.
REASONING_END

evaluated.name: Cheap With Near-Term Refinancing Cliff
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(dlc, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A depressed equity price is self-reinforcing when a large share of a firm's debt matures within the year and its current assets cannot retire it: management must refinance or issue equity at exactly the moment the market values it least, transferring value to creditors and new investors, so deep-discount firms facing a rollover cliff should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning:
The trap channel here is debt *maturity timing* rather than cash-flow weakness, so it is not the mirror of the coverage-based proposal and not a sign-flipped financial-strength score — a profitable, well-covered firm can still face a rollover cliff, and that is precisely the case this signal isolates. Current debt scaled by current assets is a rollover-capacity ratio with a positive denominator and near-universal coverage, and its interaction with book-to-market targets the situation where equity dilution risk is highest.
REASONING_END
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Maintenance-Adjusted Cash Flow To Total Claims
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(oancf, 5), TS_SUM(dp, 5)), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The cash a firm can actually distribute over a cycle is its operating cash flow less the capital it consumes in generating it, and that surplus should be compared with every claim outstanding; a firm priced low relative to five years of maintenance-adjusted cash surplus is cheap on sustainable distributable cash, while one whose cash flow merely replaces depreciating assets is not.
evaluated.reasoning:
Deducting five years of depreciation from five years of operating cash flow is the quality adjustment that separates genuine surplus from capital-consumption treadmills, which is exactly what an EBITDA-based enterprise multiple ignores. The denominator is market capitalisation plus total liabilities with no cash subtraction, so it is strictly positive for every firm and the sign-flip outliers that afflicted the net-of-cash denominator cannot arise.
REASONING_END

evaluated.name: Net Cash Cheapness With Dual Quality Screen
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), RATIO(act, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Profitability and asset liquidity are distinct guarantees behind a discounted price — one says the business earns, the other says the assets are convertible — and a cheap, cash-rich firm that offers both is much less likely to be a trap than one offering either alone.
evaluated.reasoning: Both quality channels have independently produced positive FF5 alpha against different valuation legs, so combining them into a single ranked quality composite tests whether their information is additive or redundant. Using SUMRANK inside one industry rank avoids compounding two multiplicative shrinkages, which would otherwise concentrate the long leg in an unstably small corner of the cross-section.

evaluated.name: Net Liquid Claim Cheapness With Gross Profit
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The shareholder's hard claim is current assets less every liability — receivables, inventory and cash that could in principle be realised against obligations — and a firm priced low relative to that net liquid claim while still earning gross profit is mispriced rather than distressed.
evaluated.reasoning: This upgrades the valuation leg from cash-versus-financial-debt to the full Graham net-current-asset claim, which unlike the earlier flagged che-minus-lt construction is genuinely two-sided in the cross-section because current assets are of comparable magnitude to total liabilities for most firms. Holding the profitability leg fixed against the archive's net-cash version isolates whether the alpha comes from cash specifically or from any unencumbered liquid claim.

evaluated.name: Cheapness Backed By Working Liquid Assets
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(revt, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Liquid assets support a low valuation only when they are actually turning: receivables that get collected and inventory that sells are convertible value, while a large current-asset balance that generates little revenue is stale inventory and uncollectible receivables that will be written down.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive shows B/M times the *level* of asset liquidity earns positive alpha, but level cannot distinguish convertible working assets from accumulating dead ones; replacing the level with current-asset turnover tests directly which interpretation drives the result. The pair of signals is jointly diagnostic — if turnover works better, the mechanism is realisability of book value, if the level works better, it is balance-sheet safety.

evaluated.name: Rich Price On A Strained Balance Sheet
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(lt, act)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The most reliably overpriced firms are those whose market value already embeds optimistic growth while their obligations tower over their liquid resources; when expectations disappoint, these firms must recapitalise from a position of weakness, so richly priced and illiquid balance sheets should earn low returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Both prior short-side attempts carried a high-book-to-market or liabilities-to-price leg whose unconditional cross-sectional slope is positive, which fought the negative expected sign and produced wrong-signed Fama-MacBeth t-stats despite correct-signed alphas; orienting the valuation leg toward expensiveness aligns both statistics on the same side. The quality leg, total liabilities relative to current assets, is a stock-based strain measure rather than a flow measure, so it identifies firms that cannot cover claims from realisable assets even if current earnings look adequate.

evaluated.name: Net Cash Cheapness With Accrual Conservatism
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, lct), 1), dp), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cash-rich, low-debt firm trading at a discount is mispriced when its reported profits are not being manufactured by working-capital build-up; if the same balance-sheet cheapness comes with heavy accruals, the cash position is a snapshot that operating reversals will erode.
evaluated.reasoning:
Instead of substituting a proxy inside an archived signal, this pairs the valuation leg that has generated every positive FF5 alpha in the archive with the one quality dimension the archive has never combined with it — the accrual-versus-cash content of earnings — which is orthogonal to RMW and absent from FF5 altogether. The accrual measure is built from balance-sheet primitives (act, lct, dp) so it does not inherit the sample restriction of the cash-flow statement, keeping coverage close to the 0.14 tier rather than the 0.09 tier.

evaluated.name: Cheapness With A Written-Down Asset Base
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(dp, 5), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Historical-cost accounting understates the value of an old, heavily depreciated asset base, so a firm that is cheap on book value while having charged five years of depreciation large relative to its current assets is cheap against an understated denominator; a firm equally cheap with a freshly capitalised asset base has no such hidden margin.
evaluated.reasoning:
This replaces the enterprise-multiple rediscovery with an accounting-conservatism channel: cumulative depreciation relative to the current asset base is an asset-vintage state, monotone and non-negative for every firm, so there is no sign discontinuity or sparse-tail dependence. The mechanism explains why some low price-to-book firms are genuinely cheap — their book denominator is stale — which is a quality-of-book story rather than a quality-of-earnings story and is not represented in HML, RMW or CMA.
REASONING_END

evaluated.name: Liquid Claim That Is Actually Distributed
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(dvc, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Liquid assets are only worth their carrying value to outside shareholders if management is willing to let cash leave the firm; a cheap, liquid balance sheet accompanied by real distributions is a verified claim, while the same balance sheet with no payout is an agency problem that the market discounts for good reason.
evaluated.reasoning: Every positive-alpha signal in the archive rewards liquid claims, but none tests whether those claims are accessible, which is the standard free-cash-flow agency objection to cash-rich value; payout intensity is the observable that resolves it. Dividends are used as a verification channel on an already-validated valuation leg rather than as a standalone yield, so this is not a restatement of the dividend-yield anomaly, and industry ranking keeps the comparison within payout-similar peer groups.

evaluated.name: Rank-Weighted Stock And Flow Claim Cheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The shareholder's claim is both a stock of unencumbered liquid assets and a recurring stream of cash earnings, and neither should dominate the other by an accident of accounting magnitude; a firm cheap on both components at once, while earning gross profit, is the strongest quality-value case.
evaluated.reasoning:
Combining the two claim components as equally weighted ranks removes the implicit one-times capitalization of the flow term that made the earlier additive version numerically indistinguishable from its balance-sheet leg, so the flow genuinely moves the ordering. This makes the test meaningful: if it beats the archived net-liquid-claim signal, the recurring-cash component adds information the stock claim misses, which is exactly the question the archive leaves open.

evaluated.name: Liquid Claim With Pricing Power
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt), 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A discounted, liquid firm is a quality-value case when it sells at a genuine markup over its own input costs, because pricing power is what allows the business to keep generating the liquidity behind the discount; a commodity business with no margin has nothing but its liquidation value and will consume it.
evaluated.reasoning:
Gross margin per dollar of sales is a pure income-statement measure of competitive position that contains no balance-sheet quantity, so unlike profit-scaled-by-liabilities it is not mechanically correlated with the valuation leg and cannot degenerate into a low-leverage screen. It is also economically different from the archived gross-profits-to-assets leg, which mixes margin with asset turnover, so a result would tell us which of the two components of profitability the trap distinction actually needs.

evaluated.name: Rich Price With Swelling Operating Assets
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(DELTA(RATIO(act, revt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: When a richly priced firm's receivables and inventory rise relative to the sales they are supposed to support, revenue is being pulled forward or goods are not selling, and the high valuation rests on a working-capital build that must unwind; such firms should underperform.
evaluated.reasoning:
The quality leg is the change in days of working capital carried per dollar of sales, an operating-efficiency deterioration measure, not growth in the long-lived asset base, so it is distinct from the asset-growth anomaly and is scaled by revenue rather than by a near-zero base. Pairing it with an expensiveness-oriented valuation leg keeps the cross-sectional slope and the portfolio alpha pointing the same way, which is where all previous short-side attempts broke down.

considered.name: Solvency-Gated Enterprise Earnings Yield
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), MUL(INDICATOR(RATIO(re, at), 0), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dltt, dlc), che), at)), -0.3)))

considered.name: Cheapness Per Unit Of Fundamental Risk

considered.name: Own-History Cheapness With Intact Margins
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5)), INDICATOR(DELTA(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3), 1), 0))

considered.name: Glamour With Working-Capital Bloat
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at), 1)))

considered.name: Multiple Agreement Cheapness

considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(oancf, ib), 0), 5))

considered.name: Obligation-Heavy Discount With Fading Margins
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5))))

considered.name: Owner Earnings Yield After Working-Capital Funding
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), MA(DELTA(SUB(act, lct), 1), 3)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)

considered.expression: SUB(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 5))

considered.name: Earned Capital Per Dollar Of Total Claims
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(re, ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: Book value that was earned and retained is evidence of a long profit history, whereas book value contributed by investors is not; a firm carrying deep retained earnings relative to the entire stack of claims on it — market equity plus all liabilities — is cheap for quality reasons, while a firm with thin or negative earned capital priced at the same multiple is cheap because it has never generated value.

considered.name: Net Cash Cheapness With Liability Coverage
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, lt), 3)))

If the alpha survives or improves, the mispricing is about balance-sheet safety rather than profitability level; if it collapses, the profitability channel was doing the work.

considered.name: Cheapness Backed By Liquid Assets
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(act, at)))
considered.hypothesis: A low price-to-book is credible when the book value sits in current assets that can be converted or redeployed, and is suspect when it sits in long-lived operating assets whose carrying value depends on the same weak business the market is discounting; asset composition therefore determines whether book value is a floor or an accounting artifact.

It also offers a cheap, high-coverage test of whether the alpha in the net-cash family generalises to liquidity of the whole asset base rather than cash specifically.

considered.name: Cheap With Interest-Free Financing Mix
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt))))
considered.hypothesis: What makes a discount dangerous is not the size of a firm's obligations but their type: trade payables and accrued expenses are interest-free, renegotiable financing that reflects supplier bargaining power, whereas interest-bearing debt carries fixed dates that can force liquidation before a mispricing corrects, so cheap firms whose liabilities are predominantly non-financial should realise the value premium.

This replaces the incoherent che-minus-lt construction with the obligation *composition* rather than its level, so the quality leg is a bounded share in [0,1] with a clear economic reading and no dependence on cash being large relative to liabilities. It tests a distinct hypothesis from the archive's net-cash signal — that the trap mechanism is the hardness of the claim, not the absence of claims — and the two together identify whether cash buffers or claim softness drive the observed alpha.

considered.name: Cheap With Compounding Earned Capital Per Share
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(re, csho), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: The quality that redeems a low valuation is per-share accumulation of earned capital: a cheap firm whose retained earnings per share have compounded over three years is quietly building shareholder value, while a cheap firm whose earned capital per share is flat or shrinking is either losing money or diluting existing holders to stay funded.

Rather than restating the net-external-financing anomaly as a standalone leg, dilution enters only through the per-share denominator of a value-creation measure, so a firm that issues shares while growing earned capital faster still scores well — the signal reads capital creation net of dilution, not issuance itself. This makes the quality state a cumulative outcome variable (retained profit per share) rather than a financing action, which is the conditioning the value-trap story actually requires.

considered.name: Cheap With Near-Term Refinancing Cliff
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(dlc, act)))
considered.hypothesis: A depressed equity price is self-reinforcing when a large share of a firm's debt matures within the year and its current assets cannot retire it: management must refinance or issue equity at exactly the moment the market values it least, transferring value to creditors and new investors, so deep-discount firms facing a rollover cliff should underperform.
considered.reasoning:
The trap channel here is debt *maturity timing* rather than cash-flow weakness, so it is not the mirror of the coverage-based proposal and not a sign-flipped financial-strength score — a profitable, well-covered firm can still face a rollover cliff, and that is precisely the case this signal isolates. Current debt scaled by current assets is a rollover-capacity ratio with a positive denominator and near-universal coverage, and its interaction with book-to-market targets the situation where equity dilution risk is highest.

considered.name: Maintenance-Adjusted Cash Flow To Total Claims
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(oancf, 5), TS_SUM(dp, 5)), ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), lt)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: The cash a firm can actually distribute over a cycle is its operating cash flow less the capital it consumes in generating it, and that surplus should be compared with every claim outstanding; a firm priced low relative to five years of maintenance-adjusted cash surplus is cheap on sustainable distributable cash, while one whose cash flow merely replaces depreciating assets is not.
considered.reasoning:
Deducting five years of depreciation from five years of operating cash flow is the quality adjustment that separates genuine surplus from capital-consumption treadmills, which is exactly what an EBITDA-based enterprise multiple ignores. The denominator is market capitalisation plus total liabilities with no cash subtraction, so it is strictly positive for every firm and the sign-flip outliers that afflicted the net-of-cash denominator cannot arise.

considered.name: Net Cash Cheapness With Dual Quality Screen
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), RATIO(act, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Profitability and asset liquidity are distinct guarantees behind a discounted price — one says the business earns, the other says the assets are convertible — and a cheap, cash-rich firm that offers both is much less likely to be a trap than one offering either alone.

considered.name: Net Liquid Claim Cheapness With Gross Profit
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: The shareholder's hard claim is current assets less every liability — receivables, inventory and cash that could in principle be realised against obligations — and a firm priced low relative to that net liquid claim while still earning gross profit is mispriced rather than distressed.
considered.reasoning: This upgrades the valuation leg from cash-versus-financial-debt to the full Graham net-current-asset claim, which unlike the earlier flagged che-minus-lt construction is genuinely two-sided in the cross-section because current assets are of comparable magnitude to total liabilities for most firms. Holding the profitability leg fixed against the archive's net-cash version isolates whether the alpha comes from cash specifically or from any unencumbered liquid claim.

considered.name: Cheapness Backed By Working Liquid Assets
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(revt, act)))
considered.hypothesis: Liquid assets support a low valuation only when they are actually turning: receivables that get collected and inventory that sells are convertible value, while a large current-asset balance that generates little revenue is stale inventory and uncollectible receivables that will be written down.
considered.reasoning: The archive shows B/M times the *level* of asset liquidity earns positive alpha, but level cannot distinguish convertible working assets from accumulating dead ones; replacing the level with current-asset turnover tests directly which interpretation drives the result. considered.name: Rich Price On A Strained Balance Sheet
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(RATIO(lt, act)))
considered.hypothesis: The most reliably overpriced firms are those whose market value already embeds optimistic growth while their obligations tower over their liquid resources; when expectations disappoint, these firms must recapitalise from a position of weakness, so richly priced and illiquid balance sheets should earn low returns.

considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(che, ADD(dltt, dlc)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, lct), 1), dp), at))))
considered.hypothesis: A cash-rich, low-debt firm trading at a discount is mispriced when its reported profits are not being manufactured by working-capital build-up; if the same balance-sheet cheapness comes with heavy accruals, the cash position is a snapshot that operating reversals will erode.

considered.name: Cheapness With A Written-Down Asset Base
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(TS_SUM(dp, 5), at)))
considered.hypothesis: Historical-cost accounting understates the value of an old, heavily depreciated asset base, so a firm that is cheap on book value while having charged five years of depreciation large relative to its current assets is cheap against an understated denominator; a firm equally cheap with a freshly capitalised asset base has no such hidden margin.

considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(dvc, at)))
considered.hypothesis: Liquid assets are only worth their carrying value to outside shareholders if management is willing to let cash leave the firm; a cheap, liquid balance sheet accompanied by real distributions is a verified claim, while the same balance sheet with no payout is an agency problem that the market discounts for good reason.

considered.name: Rank-Weighted Stock And Flow Claim Cheapness
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(MA(ADD(ib, dp), 3), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), at), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: The shareholder's claim is both a stock of unencumbered liquid assets and a recurring stream of cash earnings, and neither should dominate the other by an accident of accounting magnitude; a firm cheap on both components at once, while earning gross profit, is the strongest quality-value case.

Combining the two claim components as equally weighted ranks removes the implicit one-times capitalization of the flow term that made the earlier additive version numerically indistinguishable from its balance-sheet leg, so the flow genuinely moves the ordering. considered.name: Liquid Claim With Pricing Power
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(act, lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(MA(RATIO(SUB(revt, cogs), revt), 3)))
considered.hypothesis: A discounted, liquid firm is a quality-value case when it sells at a genuine markup over its own input costs, because pricing power is what allows the business to keep generating the liquidity behind the discount; a commodity business with no margin has nothing but its liquidation value and will consume it.

critic_notes.rationale: EBITDA/EV and cash conversion are both individually familiar, but the capital-structure-neutral multiple paired with a three-year OCF/EBITDA screen is a defensible and reasonably specific value-trap filter, though the conversion ratio is unstable for near-zero or negative EBITDA and needs a sign/denominator guard.

critic_notes.target_name: Weakest-Link Cheap And Profitable
critic_notes.rationale: The MIN operator is a genuinely non-additive functional form whose conjunctive logic matches the stated hypothesis, though in practice it will correlate heavily with a simple value+quality average and compresses/ties the tails, so the incremental content over a standard double-sort is the open empirical question.

critic_notes.target_name: Solvency-Weighted Cash Earnings Yield
critic_notes.rationale: Despite being labeled cross-theme, this is a purely additive average of cash-earnings yield with two Altman-Z distress components (RE/AT, WC/AT), i.e., a rediscovery of value-screened-for-distress composites with no interaction at all, and the hypothesis's conditional language is not what the expression computes.

critic_notes.target_name: Volatility-Deflated Earnings Yield
critic_notes.rationale: The ratio is non-monotone across the sign of earnings — a loss-making firm with volatile ROA scores near zero (mid-rank) while a stable loss-maker scores very negative — so the expression does not implement the stated "stable earnings make a yield more valuable" hypothesis, and winsorizing at 1% does not fix the sign discontinuity from near-zero denominators.

critic_notes.target_name: Industry Sales Yield With Margin Improvement
critic_notes.rationale: Sales-to-price (Barbee) and gross profitability (Novy-Marx) are known individually, but conditioning within-industry cheapness on a five-year gross-margin trend is a reasonable and testable directional-quality refinement; verify that IND_RANK returns non-negative values so the product does not reward the doubly-bad corner.

critic_notes.target_name: Non-Cash Charge Valuation Wedge
critic_notes.rationale: The construction is internally consistent and the rank-difference does isolate a depreciation-to-price wedge that is plausibly orthogonal to HML, though the reviewer should be aware the surviving content is close to a capital-intensity/dp-to-price tilt that CMA may partially absorb.

critic_notes.target_name: Working-Capital Accrual Gated Earnings Yield
critic_notes.rationale: This is structurally the same ZSCORE(WINSOR(yield))×INDICATOR template as the archived Solvency-Gated Enterprise Earnings Yield with only the gate swapped, and the gate itself is a direct restatement of the published Sloan balance-sheet accrual anomaly (with a crude, cash-and-debt-unadjusted accrual definition).

critic_notes.target_name: Profit-Cheap Versus Asset-Cheap Mismatch
critic_notes.rationale: Differencing GP/P against AT/P mechanically nets out the price scaling and leaves something very close to gross-profits-to-assets, i.e. a rediscovery of Novy-Marx gross profitability that RMW largely spans, contradicting the claim that FF5 leaves it unpriced.

critic_notes.target_name: Improving Liquidity Cushion Value Gate
critic_notes.rationale: Self-described as a "near-controlled contrast" with the archived gated-value signal, it reuses the identical yield×indicator template with a level-to-change tweak on the gate — a cosmetic variant unlikely to flip an alpha that was negative for portfolio-composition reasons, and its gate overlaps heavily with the accrual gate proposed alongside it.

critic_notes.target_name: Own-History Cheapness With Intact Margins
critic_notes.rationale: Substituting a time-series (own-history) valuation rank for cross-sectional cheapness is a genuinely different design that plausibly escapes HML spanning, and the margin gate is coherently specified — though the margin-trend leg echoes the archived industry sales-yield signal and the TS_RANK window units should be verified.

critic_notes.target_name: Dividend Yield Per Unit Of Leverage
critic_notes.rationale: This is essentially the long-published dividend-yield anomaly divided by a bounded leverage ratio, it collapses to a large zero mass for non-payers (biasing coverage and portfolio composition), and the stated rationale references a prior signal not in the archive.

critic_notes.target_name: Ranked Obligation-Netted Value
critic_notes.rationale: This is a monotone re-ranking of the archive's existing "Obligation-Netted Fundamental To Price" with WINSOR swapped for IND_RANK — a cosmetic variant of an already-evaluated signal rather than a substantively different mechanism, and the stated goal (diagnosing whether the alpha is tail-driven) is a robustness check, not a new hypothesis.

critic_notes.target_name: Net Cash Cheapness With Real Gross Profit
critic_notes.rationale: The net-cash-to-price valuation leg is a genuinely different balance-sheet channel from the earnings- and book-based legs already tested and the conditioning story is coherent with monotone non-negative ranks, though the product will likely be dominated by the well-documented gross profitability leg, so the incremental content over Novy-Marx is uncertain.

critic_notes.target_name: Enterprise Cheapness Meets Liability Coverage
critic_notes.rationale: This is a near-duplicate of the archive's failed "Weakest-Link Cheap And Profitable" — same MIN-of-two-ranks construction with ib+dp→ebitda and oancf/at→oancf/lt substituted — so it re-tests an already-rejected conjunctive design with a highly correlated coverage proxy.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheapness Amplified By Cash-Backing Persistence
critic_notes.rationale: The persistence-count formulation of accrual conservatism is a legitimately novel quality state distinct from the level-based accruals anomaly, but the reasoning is internally wrong — a zero count collapses the product to exactly zero for a potentially large mass of firms, destroying the valuation ordering there — so the construction is less continuous than claimed.

critic_notes.target_name: Obligation-Heavy Discount With Fading Margins
critic_notes.rationale: The short-side framing and liabilities-to-price valuation leg are a reasonable economic complement to the long-side proposals and the sign is internally consistent, but the construct is close to the published distress anomaly and liabilities-to-price is mechanically correlated with book-to-market, whose unconditional sign runs opposite to the expectation.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheap With Stable Operating Margins
critic_notes.rationale: This is the third instance of the same MUL(IND_RANK cheap yield, IND_RANK margin-dynamics) template already tried unsuccessfully in the archive with only the quality leg swapped (trend/level → volatility), and a five-observation annual VOL is a very noisy stability estimate; it also cites a "volatility-deflated yield" predecessor not present in the archive.

critic_notes.target_name: All-Obligation Netted Cheapness With Gross Profit
critic_notes.rationale: Substituting total liabilities for interest-bearing debt destroys the economic content the hypothesis claims — since (che − lt) is negative and lt-dominated for almost all firms, the "cheapness" leg becomes essentially a *low*-liabilities-to-price (i.e., anti-value, low-leverage) rank rather than a net-cash yield, making this both internally inconsistent with the stated hypothesis and a one-ingredient cosmetic edit of the archive's existing net-cash-times-gross-profit signal.

critic_notes.target_name: Net Cash Cheapness With Liability Coverage
critic_notes.rationale: Swapping the RMW-spanned gross-profitability leg for cash-flow coverage of liabilities is a genuinely diagnostic, economically motivated change to the archive's best performer that isolates whether the alpha comes from a profitability channel or a balance-sheet-safety channel, though the oancf requirement will cut coverage and any coverage decline should be checked before attributing changes to the mechanism.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheap And Not Raising Outside Capital
critic_notes.rationale: The financing leg is a near-direct restatement of the published net-external-financing / net-share-issuance anomaly (Bradshaw-Richardson-Sloan, Daniel-Titman, Pontiff-Woodgate), so the interaction is likely to be driven by an already-known standalone effect rather than by the claimed value-quality conditioning, and the proposal offers no test to separate the two.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheap Cash Burners
critic_notes.rationale: High book-to-market interacted with weak operating cash flow is essentially Piotroski's high-BM × financial-strength result (and the well-documented value-premium-concentrated-among-non-distressed finding) with the sign reversed, and it is also largely the mirror image of Signal 2 in the same batch, so it adds little independent information.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheapness Backed By Liquid Assets
critic_notes.rationale: Asset-composition as a conditioner on book-to-market is a distinct and untested channel here with high coverage and correctly applied industry ranks, but act/at is a coarse, heavily industry- and size-driven proxy that may end up restating asset tangibility rather than the reliability of book value, so the construction is plausible but thin.

critic_notes.target_name: Five-Year Cash Earnings To Enterprise Claims
critic_notes.rationale: Long-run normalized cash earnings scaled by enterprise value is close to the published enterprise-multiple anomaly (Loughran-Wellman) and to Anderson-Brooks-style multi-year earnings yield, and the stated claim that the denominator is "strictly positive by construction" is false — deep net-cash firms can have mcap + lt − che ≤ 0, producing sign-flipped outliers that WINSOR on the ratio will not cleanly fix.

critic_notes.target_name: Net Cash Cheapness With Accrual-Free Coverage
critic_notes.rationale: This is a one-input substitution (oancf → ib+dp) in an archived signal with identical economics and identical structure — a cosmetic coverage-driven variant rather than a substantively different mechanism, and the accrual-vs-cash distinction it discards is precisely the earnings-quality content the archive's other signals treat as informative.

critic_notes.target_name: Net Cash Cheapness With Dual Quality Screen
critic_notes.rationale: Internally consistent and thoughtfully constructed (SUMRANK avoids double multiplicative shrinkage), but it is an incremental blend of two already-tested legs whose quality inputs are likely correlated, so the additivity test is worth running yet unlikely to be a large step forward.

critic_notes.target_name: Net Liquid Claim Cheapness With Gross Profit
critic_notes.rationale: The valuation leg is essentially Graham's net-current-asset-value, a long-documented anomaly, but gating it on averaged gross profitability and contrasting it directly against the archived net-cash version is a legitimate and well-specified discrimination test rather than a plain rediscovery.

critic_notes.target_name: Enterprise Price Per Dollar Of Gross Profit
critic_notes.rationale: This is a direct rediscovery of the published enterprise-multiple anomaly (Loughran–Wellman), and the negative-EV rationale is shaky because the signal is non-monotone in cheapness — near-zero-EV firms rank mid-sample while the extreme long tail is populated by the sparse negative-EV cases the construct is being justified by.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheapness Backed By Working Liquid Assets
critic_notes.rationale: A coherent and genuinely diagnostic contrast to the archived B/M × current-asset-level signal, though revt/act is close to standard asset-turnover quality (an F-score ingredient) and is mechanically negatively related to act/at, so a result could partly just invert the earlier finding rather than explain it.

critic_notes.target_name: Rich Price On A Strained Balance Sheet
critic_notes.rationale: The sign diagnosis of prior short-side failures is the most intelligent reasoning in this batch and the expression's direction matches the stated hypothesis, but the glamour-plus-leverage combination is close to the documented distress/leverage-with-growth effect, and multiplying two [0,1] ranks leaves the long (low-value) leg an uninterpretable mix of cheap-and-strained with expensive-and-unstrained firms.

critic_notes.target_name: Liquid Claim Plus Earning Power Cheapness
critic_notes.rationale: The valuation leg adds an annual flow (3-yr average cash earnings) to a balance-sheet stock (act − lt) with an arbitrary implicit capitalization weight of 1x, and since the stock term is typically an order of magnitude larger and drives the cross-sectional dispersion, the signal is likely a near-duplicate of the archived "Net Liquid Claim Cheapness With Gross Profit" (identical quality leg, fmb 3.77 / alpha 2.2%) rather than a genuine test of whether the quality screen repaired the obligation-netted slope.

critic_notes.target_name: Liquid Claim With Obligation-Scaled Profit
critic_notes.rationale: This is a denominator swap (at → lt) on the quality leg of an already-archived signal, and worse, it re-introduces 1/lt into a signal whose valuation leg already nets lt, so the two legs become mechanically correlated and the "profit per dollar of obligation" leg largely proxies low leverage — a screen the archive has tested repeatedly.

critic_notes.target_name: Liquid Claim That Is Actually Distributed
critic_notes.rationale: Payout as verification that a liquid balance sheet is actually accessible to outside shareholders is a genuine free-cash-flow agency channel untested in the archive and not merely a restatement of dividend yield, though the reviewer should watch for a large tied mass of zero-dividend firms compressing the quality leg and for confounding with size/maturity.

critic_notes.target_name: Rich Price Funding Illiquid Asset Build
critic_notes.rationale: The quality leg is growth in non-current assets, which is essentially the published asset-growth anomaly (Cooper–Gulen–Schill) whose documented concentration among richly priced firms makes the interaction a rediscovery rather than a new mechanism, and GROWTH on a base that can be near zero adds instability.

critic_notes.target_name: Liquid Assets To Price With Light Obligations
critic_notes.rationale: The stated hypothesis is a diagnostic decomposition ("which component drives the alpha") rather than an economic mechanism, and the resulting construct is simply cheap-on-current-assets times low-leverage — a standard and much-studied value×leverage tilt that closely overlaps the archived ceq/mktcap × act/at signal.

critic_notes.target_name: Liquid Claim Tested Through The Cycle
critic_notes.rationale: The through-cycle minimum is a legitimately novel durability concept, but TS_MIN((act−lt)/at,5) is highly correlated with the current (act−lt) that already forms the numerator of the valuation leg, so the product is closer to squaring one balance-sheet quantity than to gating value on an independent quality dimension.

critic_notes.target_name: Claim Cheapness With Survival Horizon
critic_notes.rationale: A clean, internally consistent pairing of the archive's two best-performing legs (the stock-and-flow claim yield and the che/cogs runway screen) with genuinely distinct inputs, though it is a recombination of existing components rather than a new mechanism, so the incremental information over the two parents may be small.

critic_notes.target_name: Claim Cheapness With Profit And Runway
critic_notes.rationale: This is essentially Signal 1 with gross profitability averaged into the quality rank — a cosmetic superset that structurally repeats the archived "Net Cash Cheapness With Dual Quality Screen" template, and equal-weight rank blending will dilute rather than isolate whichever leg is actually driving the alpha.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheapness With Working Capital Runway
critic_notes.rationale: The stated mechanism (survival horizon) does not match what (act−lct)/cogs measures — net working capital is largely inventory and receivables, i.e. the same bloat that the archive's working-capital and accrual signals price *negatively* — so the expected positive sign is economically contestable and the construction is otherwise a one-input tweak of the archived cash-runway signal.

critic_notes.target_name: Cheapness With Cash Beyond Precautionary Need
critic_notes.rationale: Scaling cash by the firm's own cash-flow volatility to separate excess from precautionary cash is the only genuinely new economic state variable in the batch, ranking neutralises the ratio's fat tail, and it sits close to but not on top of the known cash-holdings/idiosyncratic-volatility literature — worth testing, with the caveat that the 5-year VOL requirement will bite coverage and the result may partly reload on low-volatility exposure.

critic_notes.target_name: Gross Profit Yield With Survival Horizon
critic_notes.rationale: A legitimate portability test of the runway channel against the valuation leg that has repeatedly shown strong FMB slopes with zero FF5 alpha, but it shares the entire quality leg with Signal 1 and the GP/P × IND_RANK(quality) template has already failed on alpha five times in this archive, so the prior is weak.

critic_notes.target_name: Rich Price With Debt Due And No Cash
critic_notes.rationale: The short-side orientation and the dlc/che rollover ratio are correctly signed and coherently motivated as a fix for the sign misalignment in the archived refinancing-cliff test, but it recombines two archived signals' parts and dlc/che is undefined or explosive for near-zero-cash firms, which will concentrate the short leg in a small, unstable set that IND_RANK only partly tames.

critic_notes.target_name: Claim Cheapness Against Total Call On Cash
critic_notes.rationale: Because cogs typically dwarfs total debt for the vast majority of firms, che/(cogs+debt) ranks almost identically to the archived che/cogs gate, making this a cosmetic re-scaling of the existing champion rather than an economic unification.

critic_notes.target_name: Claim Cheapness With Cash Free Of Near-Term Claims
critic_notes.rationale: The gross-versus-net liquidity distinction is a genuine and testable economic refinement of the runway gate, but note that lct is already netted inside the (act − lt) valuation leg, so the two legs partially double-count the same balance-sheet quantity and a positive result will be hard to attribute cleanly.

critic_notes.target_name: Stock Claim Cheapness With Survival Horizon
critic_notes.rationale: This is a pure drop-one ablation of the archived champion that simply recombines two already-tested legs (act−lt cheapness and che/cogs runway), so while diagnostically useful it is too mechanically derivative to count as a new signal.

critic_notes.target_name: Rich Price With A Funding Gap
critic_notes.rationale: The re-specification of the rollover gap as a bounded, asset-scaled difference is internally consistent with the negative expected sign and is motivated by a credible diagnosis of why the earlier ratio-based version had a strong alpha but a flat cross-sectional slope.

critic_notes.target_name: Claim Cheapness With Through-Cycle Runway
critic_notes.rationale: Swapping the current runway level for its five-year minimum on the champion's valuation leg is a predictable interpolation of two already-tested signals, and the stated claim that the legs share no accounting quantity is wrong since che sits inside act and debt inside lt.

critic_notes.target_name: Claim Cheapness With Share Count Shrinking
critic_notes.rationale: The conditioning variable is essentially the well-documented net share issuance/repurchase anomaly, so the product will largely inherit a known published effect and any result will be difficult to attribute to the proposed valuation-liquidity interaction.

critic_notes.target_name: Claim Cheapness With Cash After Commitments
critic_notes.rationale: The archive already contains gross cash (che/cogs, +6.3%), cash net of all current liabilities ((che−lct)/cogs, +5.0%) and cash against total debt (che/(dltt+dlc), +4.9%) on the identical valuation leg, so netting out dlc+dvc is a third interpolation point on the same continuum rather than a new mechanism, and the dvc term adds little since dividends are small relative to cogs for most firms.

critic_notes.target_name: Consensus Cheapness With Survival Horizon
critic_notes.rationale: Merging the highest-slope leg (gross-profit yield) with the highest-alpha leg under the same runway gate is a substantively motivated attempt to resolve a documented FMB/alpha divergence, though the nested SUMRANK weights the claim channel roughly half and the two earnings channels a quarter each — not the "three equally weighted ranks" the reasoning claims — and gross profit and cash earnings are highly collinear, so the incremental information may be smaller than advertised.

critic_notes.target_name: Claim Cheapness With Extended Runway
critic_notes.rationale: Converting the runway gate from a pure stock to stock-plus-flow is an economically sensible fix for the "buffer being drained vs replenished" blind spot, but MA(ib+dp,3) already drives the valuation leg, so the gate partly re-weights the same profitability variable and the expression risks becoming a quadratic in cash earnings rather than an independent conditioning state.

critic_notes.target_name: Unforced Cheapness Minus Forced Richness
critic_notes.rationale: This is a mechanical linear combination of two already-evaluated archive signals rather than a new hypothesis, and the subtraction is not economically clean — the short component carried an insignificant FMB slope (t=−0.54) and both terms are non-negative rank products whose difference is dominated by whichever leg has the wider dispersion, so any gain would reflect portfolio blending, not a tested mechanism.

critic_notes.target_name: Claim Cheapness With Self-Funding Operations
critic_notes.rationale: Holding the denominator and units of the winning gate fixed while swapping the cash stock for the cash flow is a genuine discrimination test that can falsify the "unforced transaction" story against a plain profitability-scaling story, and either outcome is informative; the main caveat is the shared MA(ib+dp,3) term with the valuation leg.

critic_notes.target_name: Additive Unforced Cheapness Score
critic_notes.rationale: Isolating the combination operator (complements vs substitutes) on the archive's best ingredients is a legitimate structural question the archive has not addressed, but it sits close to a cosmetic re-parameterisation of the champion, and the nested SUMRANK again yields unequal channel weights that undercut the stated "three equally weighted channels" design.

critic_notes.target_name: Four-Channel Unforced Cheapness Score
critic_notes.rationale: This is the literal union of two archived signals — "Additive Unforced Cheapness Score" (claim + cash earnings + runway) and the gross-profit channel from "Consensus Cheapness With Survival Horizon" — so it is an incremental re-nesting rather than a new mechanism, and with four highly correlated price-scaled channels the marginal information from the added leg is likely near zero.

critic_notes.target_name: Consensus Cheapness With Dual Cash Gate
critic_notes.rationale: The two "demands" being combined share the same numerator (che) and are therefore strongly correlated, so the additive gate is close to a monotone transform of the archived runway gate; additionally the claim that coverage is preserved at 0.118 is doubtful since the che/(dltt+dlc) component already cost the archived creditor-proof variant coverage (0.106) through zero/missing-debt denominators.

critic_notes.target_name: High-Coverage Consensus With Survival Horizon
critic_notes.rationale: The motivating premise is factually wrong — the binding coverage constraint is the (act − lt) claim term, which caps archived act−lt signals at ~0.121, not the MA(ib+dp,3) term, so dropping cash earnings buys at best 0.003 of coverage while discarding a channel that the archive shows carries alpha.

critic_notes.target_name: Signed Cheapness With A Funding Gap
critic_notes.rationale: This is a defensible construction fix for a genuinely diagnosed slope/alpha divergence (non-negative rank products give the FMB regression no signed variation), and the expected negative sign matches the expression's direction, though the un-winsorized IND_ZSCORE of a market-cap-scaled claim yield is severely fat-tailed and will let a handful of micro-cap outliers dominate the cross-sectional slope.

critic_notes.target_name: Consensus Cheapness With Cash Intensity
critic_notes.rationale: A clean, honestly framed ablation that discriminates "survival horizon" from a plain cash-holdings effect (itself a known published anomaly, Palazzo 2012), which limits novelty but makes the test genuinely informative about which mechanism drives the archive's champions.

critic_notes.target_name: Consensus Cheapness Free On Both Sides
critic_notes.rationale: The two gate components are economically and statistically complementary (asset-side runway with the largest alpha, liability-side maturity absence with the largest slope) rather than redundant like the dual-cash version, the coverage argument is correct since dlc/at is defined for debt-free firms, and the expression matches the stated hypothesis and sign.
